t: Old Turkic, the earliest recorded Turkic language, was first written in the 8th century on the stone monuments of the Second Turkic Khaganate in the Orkhon valley of Mongolia, in an alphabet resembling runes.

The Uyghurs, who succeeded the Turks on the steppe and settled in the oases of the Tarim Basin, wrote a large literature in it, Buddhist, Manichaean and Christian, much of it recovered from the sands of Turfan and the caves of Dunhuang.
The Turkic languages, which spread from Mongolia to the Balkans, are spoken today by some 200 million people, who honour the Orkhon inscriptions as the beginning of their written history.
dyk: The memorial stone of the Turkic prince Kul Tigin, raised in 732, carries an inscription in Old Turkic runes on three sides and, on the fourth, a Chinese text composed by the Tang emperor Xuanzong.
ev: Bumin founds the Turkic Khaganate, the first state to bear the name Türk
The adviser Tonyukuk sets up the first of the great Old Turkic inscriptions in Mongolia
The memorial inscription of Kul Tigin is raised in the Orkhon valley
The Uyghur khagan adopts Manichaeism, whose texts are translated into Old Turkic
The fall of the Uyghur Khaganate drives the Uyghurs to the oases of Turfan and Gansu
Yusuf Khass Hajib completes the Kutadgu Bilig, the first great Islamic work in Turkic
Mahmud al-Kashgari writes his Compendium of the Languages of the Turks in Baghdad
Vilhelm Thomsen deciphers the Old Turkic runic script

f.family: Turkic: the earliest recorded member of the family, close to the common ancestor of most Turkic languages
f.script: The Old Turkic runic script; later the Old Uyghur script, derived from Sogdian, and other scripts, including Arabic
f.earliest: The Orkhon inscriptions of the Second Turkic Khaganate in Mongolia, about 720 to 735
f.status: Extinct; its relatives and successors, the Turkic languages, among them Turkish, Azerbaijani, Uzbek, Kazakh, Uyghur and Tatar, are spoken by some 200 million people
